# Tools

## Understanding Tools

Agents become tremendously more powerful when we also give them **tools**. Think of **tools** as traditional software that an agent can use in conjunction with the LLM. Why would we need tools? 

1. In the workflow you were working on, click the back button until you get to the Add Tasks stage. If you already closed the workflow you can get back to editing it from the drafts on the homepage of Agent Studio.   
2. Modify the task as below. Make sure you click Save Task.   
     
     
   **Task Description:** Create a birthday message that is only one sentence. Make sure that it is only one sentence. Double check this before returning the output. Also count the number of characters just in the birthday message.   
   **Expected Output:** One sentence birthday message. The number of characters in the message. Nothing additional.   
     
     
   ![][image15]  
     
3. Now go forward to the Test stage and run the workflow again. Did the LLM accurately count the characters? Check here\! [https://wordcounter.net/character-count](https://wordcounter.net/character-count)  
     
   ![][image16]  
   

Hopefully this provides some intuition at what LLMs are good at. Remember LLMs are glorified autocomplete. It just turns out that human language systems are basically the same thing just with lots of training data and some wicked efficiency to filter out noise. 

Why might language models struggle to count characters? Put your answer in the Zoom Chat.

What is good at counting characters? Well you actually used a **tool,** traditional deterministic software to verify the results. 

When you combine agents with tools, they become an order of magnitude more powerful, because they can combine the language skills of LLMs with other kinds of capabilities. 

**Building a Custom Tool**

Now lets build a character count tool to solve this problem. 

1. Exit the workflow editing page by clicking on Tool Catalog. Your workflow will be saved and accessible from the home page. Create a new tool and name it CharacterCount. Click Edit Tool File and a new tab will open in the CAI workbench.   
     
     
2. Click edit next to the [tool.py](http://tool.py) file in the file browser. There is no need to start a session.  
   

3. Read the code in the file. This file is a template for a tool and is well commented to explain what a tool should look like.   
   ![][image17]  
     
4. Now delete the code that is there and copy and paste this code block.

"""  
This tool counts the number of characters in some text and returns the count.   
"""

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field  
from typing import Optional, Any  
import json   
import argparse

class UserParameters(BaseModel):  
    """  
    Parameters used to configure a tool. This may include API keys,  
    database connections, environment variables, etc.  
     
    """  
    pass

class ToolParameters(BaseModel):  
    """  
    Arguments of a tool call. These arguments are passed to this tool whenever  
    an Agent calls this tool. The descriptions below are also provided to agents  
    to help them make informed decisions of what to pass to the tool.  
    input2: str \= Field(description="Second parameter to be passed to the tool")  
    """  
    input1: str \= Field(description="The text that needs to be counted for characters.")

def run\_tool(config: UserParameters, args: ToolParameters) \-\> Any:  
    """  
    Main tool code logic. Anything returned from this method is returned  
    from the tool back to the calling agent.  
    """

    return len(args.input1)

OUTPUT\_KEY \= "tool\_output"  
"""  
When an agent calls a tool, technically the tool's entire stdout can be passed back to the agent.  
However, if an OUTPUT\_KEY is present in a tool's main file, only stdout content \*after\* this key is  
passed to the agent. This allows us to return structured output to the agent while still retaining  
the entire stdout stream from a tool\! By default, this feature is enabled, and anything returned  
from the run\_tool() method above will be the structured output of the tool.  
"""

if \_\_name\_\_ \== "\_\_main\_\_":  
    """  
    Tool entrypoint.   
      
    The only two things that are required in a tool are the  
    ToolConfiguration and ToolArguments classes. Then, the only two arguments that are  
    passed to a tool entrypoint are "--tool-config" and "--tool-args", respectively. The rest  
    of the implementation is up to the tool builder \- feel free to customize the entrypoint to your   
    chosing\!  
    """  
      
    parser \= argparse.ArgumentParser()  
    parser.add\_argument("--user-params", required=True, help="Tool configuration")  
    parser.add\_argument("--tool-params", required=True, help="Tool arguments")  
    args \= parser.parse\_args()  
      
    \# Parse JSON into dictionaries  
    user\_dict \= json.loads(args.user\_params)  
    tool\_dict \= json.loads(args.tool\_params)  
      
    \# Validate dictionaries against Pydantic models  
    config \= UserParameters(\*\*user\_dict)  
    params \= ToolParameters(\*\*tool\_dict)  
      
    \# Run the tool.  
    output \= run\_tool(config, params)  
    print(OUTPUT\_KEY, output)

—---

What changes did we make from the template? First we edited the description of the tool. It is very important that we provide a good description so that our LLM can figure out when to use the tool. Then we edited the UserParameters class. We don’t need to pass any configuration parameters so we removed all the sample ones. Then we edited the input arguments and provided a description of them for the LLM to understand what needs to be passed into the tool. Finally we implement the logic to actually count characters of the input parameter. 

5. When you are done implementing these changes click file save and return to the agent studio tab. Click refresh to update the code preview and you will see your new code there. Save the tool. 

Congrats on creating your first tool\! Now Take a look at how CrewAI interacts with the LLM to actually use the tool.

![][image18]  
![][image19]  
![][image20]

CrewAI tells the model about all the class variables in ToolParmaters and provides the model the description of each variable. It also provides the tool description which we configured earlier. The way in which we provide context about a model is similar to the way we might walk a colleague through an unfamiliar codebase.  CrewAI needs the tools to be written in a very standard way in order to do that. However not everyone is going to write new tools for every single agent framework. We need some way to standardize how we give tool context to agents.  HEAVY FORSHADOWING…

Creating your own tool is one example of how AI Studios are both High and Low code applications at the same time. More technical users might create tools, well business users might simply use them to build workflows. 

Now let's give your agent this tool in order to get an accurate character count. 

1. Go to the home page of AgentStudio, you can easily do so using the breadcrumb navigation with the home icon. Click on the OneAgent Workflow and click edit. 

2. Edit your agent and under Add Optional Tools click Create or Edit Tools. Search for the CharacterCount tool, select it and click create new tool. This copies the tool template we created earlier for this specific agent. Click Save Tool and close the create or edit tools modal. Click Save Agent and close the modal. You should now see the tool added to your workflow.   
     
   ![][image21]  
     
   ![][image22]  
     
3. Test the workflow and check if with the tool you can now get an accurate character count. 

## Understanding MCP

What if we wanted to post our fantastic birthday message to X/Twitter to show our dear friend just how much we care. This is surely a very common problem. There are several Python packages that can abstract away dealing with that pesky Twitter API. However they aren’t written for CrewAI. How will the model understand the context of these tools and how will the code actually be executed? 

Near the end of 2024 Anthropic released an open source protocol called MCP that allows for you to write a tool once and have it used by all the different agent frameworks. 

**Lets take a look at MCP and how it works in the context of AgentStudio**

Agent Studio is known as an MCP Host. It is an application that wants to provide context to its AI models. 

Agent Studio has an implementation of the MCP client which connects to MCP Servers in a 1:1 fashion. The host will have an instance of the client for each server. 

An external developer will write an MCP Server once for their tools and it can be used by any Host who implements the MCP client, including Agent Studio. 

![][image23]

Interestingly enough the MCP Servers themselves, despite being implemented by the tool provider, are actually hosted by AgentStudio. While MCP Servers can be hosted externally this is not something supported yet by AgentStudio. 

The other neat thing about MCP is that it is designed to not just expose tools but also data and prompts. Different MCP clients have different support for these features. For now let's just focus on tools. 

.  
**\`Future of MCP**

MCP is starting to see rapid adoption which has in turn spurred ISVs to start writing MCP Servers for their software. Cloudera itself is one of those ISVs that is starting to create servers so that Agents can build with Cloudera’s data platform. For example this server to access iceberg tables via impala: [https://github.com/cloudera/iceberg-mcp-server](https://github.com/cloudera/iceberg-mcp-server)

**Using MCP In Agent Studio**

If we want to have our agents post to Twitter instead of adapting some Python twitter tool for CrewAI we can simply use any MCP compatible twitter tool and add it to Agent Studio. 

1. Take a look at this open source MCP server: [https://github.com/EnesCinr/twitter-mcp](https://github.com/EnesCinr/twitter-mcp)  
     
2. Copy the setup JSON from the quickstart  
   ![][image24]  
     
3. In AgentStudio go to the Tools Catalog, MCP Servers and click register.   
     
4. Paste the JSON into the pop up, deleting what was already there. 

   

5. Change the name of twitter-mcp key to just twitter and click Register. DO NOT change the args: value. It should still be @enescinar/twitter-mcp. The MCP Server will be imported and validated. It should look like this   
     
   

**What does this JSON do?** 

There are two types of MCP servers supported by Agent Studio- Node JS based server and Python based server. The command value for a node server is always npx and for python it's uvx. You might recognize the npx command if you have done backend web development. It is a command from the NPM package manager and runs a [node.js](http://node.js) program locally without globally installing it. UVX is a similar command from a different package manager. It is from the relatively new UV package manager which you can think of as a modern replacement for PIP or Conda.  

All the arguments in the args key get passed into these commands which Agent Studio executes.  You can specify additional configuration and importantly what package to run. You specify the name of the package as it exists in the public repository and the package manager pulls it. In the case of the Node ecosystem this is any package listed on the NPM registry and from Python it is any package from PyPi package index. 

Here is the link to the NPM registry package we are actually pulling.  [https://www.npmjs.com/package/@enescinar/twitter-mcp](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@enescinar/twitter-mcp).

Agent Studio plays the role of both Server and Client by running these Sever packages and having its Agents call them.

## Multi Agent Systems & Agentic Workflows

What if you have a larger objective that you want to accomplish that is composed of multiple tasks? 

You could assign these tasks all to a single agent, however much like the real world there is an advantage to having specific agents specialize. Much like people excel in certain areas, agents can be made to do the same by giving them access to fine tuned LLMs for specific tasks. Multiple agents working together is called a **Multi Agent System.** 

Also we need to consider what order the tasks should be executed. Tasks may need to be executed in a specific sequence or executed in parallel for efficiency to achieve a specific goal. There is a specific **workflow** that needs to be executed in order to achieve a larger goal. Well humans can manually orchestrate these workfolks we can actually assign an orchestrator agent to plan the workflow autonomously. This is called an **agentic workflow.** 

## Building A Multi Agent Workflow

Now that we have our Twitter MCP Server installed we need to assign it to an agent so it can post our birthday wish. One option is to give our existing agent access to the Twitter MCP Server and assign it a secondary task. Alternatively we can build a new dedicated agent whose sole mission is to post messages to Twitter and set up a multi agent workflow such that both agents work together to complete the larger mission.
